newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl faces rough political ride with Buba gold grab. [CORRECTED 16:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Kohl faces rough political ride with Buba gold grab. [CORRECTED 16:05 GMT]

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl faces a turbulent political ride in coming weeks if he overrules one of Germany's most respected institutions, the Bundesbank, for the unpopular goal of securing Europe's single currency.

The gamble is unlike any other risk that Kohl, until now arguably the most influential politician in Germany and Europe, has taken in his record-breaking 14 years in office. If it goes wrong, Bonn insiders say, it could cost him his job.

Even if Kohl succeeds in revaluing Bundesbank gold to help Bonn qualify for Europe's monetary union (EMU), the loss of credibility at home and abroad could cripple the legendary "Kohl system" that has kept him in power for so long.
"He may have lost the 1998 election right there," remarked one Bonn insider, who asked not to be named. "Even if he hasn't lost it, the whole ball game has changed."

Desperate to start EMU in 1999, Kohl did the unthinkable on Wednesday by telling the Bundesbank he would cut it down to size by changing the law and making it pay cash-strapped Bonn up to 20 billion marks ($11 billion) from the revalued gold.

The bank, which until then Bonn had presented as the model of fierce independence that Europe's future central bank must follow, had only minutes earlier rejected the gold plan as a threat to the euro and interference in its independence.
Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel lost the battle for public opinion within hours of the gold war breaking out.
Initial comments in the press ran heavily against any "creative accounting" for EMU and expressed shock that they might tamper with the bank that stability-minded Germans trust most.

The next showdown could come soon, when he has to win support to change the Bundesbank law from reluctant Christian Democrat (CDU) deputies who got an earful of criticism in their home districts during this long Corpus Christi holiday weekend.

"He has the parliamentary majority to change the law, but what political price will we have to pay for that?" a CDU official asked. "I used to think this option was like those medieval torture instruments you showed but never used."
Looking further ahead, the chancellor will also have to break the hitherto firm grip his two smaller coalition partners have had on key elements in the drive to qualify for EMU.

The liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) has sworn not to allow tax hikes to make up for budget shortfalls while the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) has insisted on the tightest possible interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for EMU. (corrects to delete reference to Waigel who belongs to the CSU party and not to the Free Democrats)

Nobody in Bonn believes the small FDP will be able to hold back the tide if Waigel, as expected, opts to raise petrol taxes this summer. The FDP has only one last shot -- quitting the coalition -- but nobody believes that will happen either.

The strains over EMU have also exposed the CSU link that has forced Waigel, chairman of the conservative Catholic party, to repeat the motto "three percent is three percent" daily as if it were a decade of Hail Marys in a rosary.

Waigel's main CSU rival, Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, has nailed him to this cross, forcing him to insist that budget deficits cannot go one pfenning above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) even though many economists and politicians say Maastricht allows some leeway.

Stoiber, who wants to steal the mantle of CSU chairman from Waigel, has a two-fold strategy, Bonn political sources say -- to reassure his sceptical voters that EMU will be safe if it works and pin the blame on Waigel if the euro backfires.
In a rare political swipe, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke publicly accused Bonn of failing to convince voters on EMU and letting Bavarian power struggles influence policy.
"We are being driven more by party congress resolutions in Bavaria than by what the Maastricht treaty actually says," he told German Radio on Wednesday evening.

The atmosphere is now so charged that pundits are wondering whose head will roll first. Since Kohl's coalition leadership has closed ranks firmly around Waigel, the focus has turned to Frankfurt and Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer.

The bank denied market rumours on Wednesday that Tietmeyer, originally a Kohl protege, had resigned. ARD TV commented in the evening: "Today, Tietmeyer denied he was going to quit." The commentator then added for emphasis: "Today..."
